titulo.texto: Ixtle Utensils and Basketry from Maguey

frase_gancho.texto: From the maguey come thread, rope, bags, and needles.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the work of the hands, we move on to prayer. Look for a stepped altar with crosses dressed in embroidered cloth, flowers, candles, and a clay incense burner.

guion_corto.texto: These objects are made of ixtle, the fiber of the maguey, the most important plant of the highlands. To extract it, the thick leaves are scraped until the threads come apart, and then the threads are washed, dried, and braided. You will see ayates, which are carrying cloths; shoulder bags, ropes, brushes, and other everyday tools. The Otomi of the Mezquital Valley, a dry region with little rain, have made the maguey into nearly everything: roof, food, drink, medicine, and clothing. Ixtle is tough but flexible, and from it people make everything from heavy carrying ropes to soft blankets. These objects show how, with patience, a person can live from a single plant.

guion_largo.texto:
Imagine that you could choose only one plant to survive. Many peoples of the highlands would choose the maguey. And that is no exaggeration: from the maguey come fiber for making rope, bags, and clothing; aguamiel, a sweet sap that is drunk just as it is or left to ferment into pulque; the worm that is eaten; the leaf that serves as a roof; and even a needle with thread, because the thorn at the tip is pulled off with a thread attached.

What you see here is the fiber, the ixtle. It is the same fiber you already saw in the [bundles from Candelaria Cave](mna_s11_fardo_candelaria) and in the hair of the [Viejitos (Little Old Men) mask](mna_s14_mascara_viejitos). It is obtained by scraping the leaves until only the threads remain. It is hard work, done by hand and learned from girlhood. Afterward the fiber is washed, dried in the sun, and spun with a clay spindle.

The Otomi of the Mezquital Valley live in a dry region of mesquite trees and magueys. The name “Mezquital” comes from a Nahuatl word for the mesquite. In a place where it rains little, the maguey withstands drought and provides food, drink, and clothing. That capacity to make use of everything is what is often called ecological wisdom: living well without exhausting what surrounds you.

Look at the ayate, that kind of netted cloth. It is used to carry corn, firewood, fruit, and also babies. It is worn on the back, held by a tumpline, a band that rests on the forehead. It is the system used by the porters of ancient Mexico, the tlamemes. Without pack animals or wheels, long-distance trade, in Teotihuacán as in Paquimé, was done on foot, with people carrying the load this way, on the back and held by the forehead.

And the ayate has a special fame. According to tradition, the tilma of Juan Diego, on which the image of the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have appeared, was made of maguey fiber. It is a way of remembering that this very humble material has been present in the most important moments of the country’s history.

The maguey also had its goddess. The Mexica venerated Mayahuel, the goddess of the maguey, and believed that her children, the Four Hundred Rabbits, were gods of pulque, who presided over drunkenness and festivity. It was a sacred drink that not just anyone could take. Today pulque is still alive in many places in the highlands, though without those rules.

That is why these objects, so simple, are a lesson. Ropes, brushes, blankets: nothing you see was made in a factory. Everything came from one plant, from the work of a pair of hands, and from ancient knowledge. Today ixtle is being valued again: bags, scrubbers, and brushes are made from the fiber as an alternative to plastic. If you think about it, it is the best example of making use of nature that you will find in the whole museum.

texto: Find the ayate, the netted cloth, and the tumplines that held it
Compare the ixtle threads: which are thicker and which are finer?
Look at the brushes and the ropes: do you know what each one is for?

texto.Region: Mezquital Valley, Hidalgo and State of Mexico
texto.Technique/Material: Maguey fiber (ixtle), stripped, spun on a spindle whorl and woven on a backstrap loom
texto.Function: Agricultural carrying tools, basketry, containers and rural clothing

texto.pregunta: Myth: The maguey is only good for making pulque or tequila.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It provides fiber for rope, bags, and clothing, as well as food, drink, medicine, roofs, and even needle and thread. The Otomi of the Mezquital live from that knowledge.
